q: Fischer esterification of acetic acid with 1-butanol (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst) has K ≈ 4. Which change most increases the yield of butyl acetate?
c: Use excess 1-butanol and remove water as it forms
Add water so the acetic acid dissolves completely in the mixture
Replace H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> with NaOH as the catalyst so the acid reacts faster
Double the amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst to speed up the reaction
h: The reaction is an equilibrium with water as a product. Think Le Châtelier.
w: With K near 4, equimolar reactants stop at about 2/3 conversion. Adding excess alcohol (a reactant) and removing water (a product, e.g. with a Dean–Stark trap or drying agent) both shift the equilibrium toward ester: excess 1-butanol plus water removal.
x: Water is a product, so adding it pushes the equilibrium back toward acid and alcohol (ester hydrolysis).
NaOH deprotonates the acid to a carboxylate, which no alcohol can attack; base also hydrolyzes esters. Fischer esterification needs acid catalysis.
A catalyst speeds up the approach to equilibrium in both directions but does not change K or the equilibrium yield.

q: Benzoic acid is heated with CH<sub>3</sub><sup>18</sup>OH and a catalytic amount of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Where is the <sup>18</sup>O found once the reaction reaches equilibrium?
c: in the ester, as the O bonded to the CH<sub>3</sub> group
in the ester, as the C=O oxygen
in the water that is formed
spread equally between the ester's two oxygens
h: Which bond of the alcohol breaks: C–O or O–H? The alcohol oxygen is the nucleophile.
w: In Fischer esterification the alcohol oxygen attacks the protonated carbonyl carbon, so the CH3–18O bond is never broken. After proton transfers, one of the acid's original OH groups leaves as water. The label ends up in the ester as the C–18O–CH3 oxygen.
x: The C=O oxygen of the ester comes from the benzoic acid; the alcohol oxygen becomes the single-bonded alkoxy oxygen.
Water is formed from an oxygen of the carboxylic acid, not from the alcohol; the alcohol's C–O bond stays intact.

The tetrahedral intermediate can lose either of the acid-derived OH groups, but the alcohol-derived OCH<sub>3</sub> is retained; it cannot become the carbonyl oxygen while staying bonded to CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Ethyl acetate is heated in H<sub>2</sub><sup>18</sup>O containing H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> until hydrolysis is complete. Which product(s) contain <sup>18</sup>O?
c: acetic acid only; the ethanol contains no <sup>18</sup>O
ethanol only; the acetic acid contains no <sup>18</sup>O
neither; the label remains in the water
h: Acid hydrolysis is Fischer esterification run backward. Water attacks which atom, and which bond to oxygen breaks?
w: Labeled water adds to the protonated C=O carbon, so 18O becomes bonded to the acyl carbon. The tetrahedral intermediate then expels ethanol, breaking the acyl–O bond; the CH3CH2–O bond is never touched. So 18O ends up in acetic acid only, and the ethanol keeps its original oxygen.
x: Ethanol would carry the label only if water attacked the ethyl carbon (an S<sub>N</sub>2 at the alkyl group, alkyl–oxygen cleavage), which does not happen for a primary ethyl ester.
Ethanol's oxygen is the original ester alkoxy oxygen; its C–O bond never breaks, so the label cannot get into it.
Water is the nucleophile that adds to the carbonyl, so its oxygen is incorporated into the acid.

q: Acid-catalyzed ester hydrolysis is reversible, but saponification (ester + NaOH, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> workup) goes to completion. Why?
c: The acid formed is deprotonated by base, and the carboxylate cannot be attacked by alkoxide
Hydroxide is a better leaving group than alkoxide, so the reverse step cannot occur at all
The alkoxide leaving group is protonated by water and evaporates from the hot mixture as an alcohol
Hydroxide forms a more stable tetrahedral intermediate than water does, so the forward step is irreversible
h: Look at what happens right after the alkoxide leaves the tetrahedral intermediate. What acid and base are now together?
w: Loss of RO− gives a carboxylic acid (pKa ≈ 5) next to a strong base (RO− or HO−, conjugate-acid pKa ≈ 16). Proton transfer is essentially complete and gives a resonance-stabilized carboxylate. The carboxylate is negatively charged and the least electrophilic acyl species, so the alcohol cannot attack it to re-form the ester: the deprotonation drives the reaction to completion.
x: Hydroxide and alkoxides are similar leaving groups; the irreversibility comes from the acid–base step, not leaving-group ability.
Most alcohols do not evaporate under these conditions; the reaction is irreversible even in a closed flask.
The tetrahedral intermediate is a high-energy species in either case; its stability does not decide whether the overall reaction is reversible.

q: The ester shown (pure R) is heated with aqueous NaOH. What alcohol is obtained?
h: In saponification, which bond to the ester oxygen breaks: acyl–O or alkyl–O? Is the stereocenter's C–O bond involved?
w: Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon; the tetrahedral intermediate expels the alkoxide by breaking the acyl–O bond. The bond from oxygen to the stereocenter is never broken, so the configuration is retained: (R)-butan-2-ol.
x: Inversion would require an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack of hydroxide at the stereocenter with carboxylate leaving; saponification instead occurs at the carbonyl carbon.
Racemization would require a carbocation at the stereocenter (S<sub>N</sub>1); no C–O bond to that carbon breaks.
Saponification is not an oxidation; forming a ketone would require an oxidizing agent.

q: A carboxylic acid is converted to the acid chloride with thionyl chloride (SOCl<sub>2</sub>). What are the by-products?
w: RCO2H + SOCl2 → RCOCl + SO2 + HCl. Both by-products are gases, which leave the mixture and help drive the reaction to completion.
x: Thionyl chloride is the reagent, not a by-product, and no water forms (water would destroy the acid chloride).
Sulfur stays in the +4 state and ends up as SO<sub>2</sub>; no Cl<sub>2</sub> or sulfuric acid forms.
This is not balanced: the Cl atoms and the acid's H must go somewhere, and they leave as HCl.

q: Benzoyl chloride is treated with dimethylamine to make N,N-dimethylbenzamide. Why are at least two equivalents of dimethylamine used (when no other base is added)?
c: The second equivalent neutralizes HCl, which would otherwise protonate the amine and stop it reacting
The first equivalent attacks the carbonyl, and the second is needed to break the C–Cl bond in the intermediate
Two amine molecules must add to the C=O to form the tetrahedral intermediate
The second equivalent reduces the acid chloride to benzaldehyde before the amide forms
h: Write the by-product of acyl substitution on an acid chloride. What does it do to an amine?
w: Each acylation releases one HCl. Dimethylamine is a base, so the HCl converts it to (CH3)2NH2+ Cl−, which has no lone pair and cannot attack. With one equivalent, the yield would stop near 50%. The second equivalent (or pyridine/Et3N) is a sacrificial base for HCl.
x: Chloride leaves on its own when the tetrahedral intermediate collapses; no second amine is needed to break the C–Cl bond.
Only one amine adds to the carbonyl carbon; the tetrahedral intermediate has one N.
Amines are not reducing agents; aldehydes from acid chlorides need a hydride donor such as LiAl(OtBu)3H.

q: What is the major organic product?
h: Gilman reagents (R<sub>2</sub>CuLi) are softer and less reactive than Grignard reagents. How many times do they add to an acid chloride?
w: Lithium dimethylcuprate transfers one methyl to the acid chloride, replacing Cl and giving a ketone. It reacts with acid chlorides but only very slowly with ketones, so the reaction stops: A, 1-cyclopentylethan-1-one.
x: The 3° alcohol results from two additions, which happens with excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, not with a cuprate.
A secondary alcohol would need a hydride to reduce the ketone; no hydride source is present.
Cuprates do not reduce acid chlorides; the methyl group, not hydride, is transferred.

q: Which reagent(s) carry out the conversion shown?
h: You need exactly one hydride and a product that survives the reagent.
w: Lithium tri-tert-butoxyaluminum hydride has only one, bulky, weakly reactive hydride. At −78 °C it reduces the very reactive acid chloride but reacts only slowly with the aldehyde product, so the reduction stops there: LiAl(OtBu)3H, −78 °C.
x: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the aldehyde as fast as it forms, so the product is 2-phenylethanol.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> also reduces aldehydes rapidly, so any aldehyde formed would go on to the primary alcohol (and methanol itself reacts with the acid chloride to give an ester).
A cuprate transfers a methyl, not a hydride, giving the methyl ketone 1-phenylpropan-2-one.

q:
Benzoyl chloride is converted to ethyl benzoate with ethanol in pyridine. Which statements about pyridine are correct?
I. It neutralizes the HCl formed.
II. It can attack the acid chloride to give an acylpyridinium ion, which ethanol then attacks.
III. It must deprotonate ethanol to ethoxide before any reaction can occur.
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of pyridinium (≈ 5) with that of ethanol (≈ 16).
w: Pyridine (I) scavenges HCl as pyridinium chloride and (II) can act as a nucleophilic catalyst, forming a highly electrophilic acylpyridinium ion. Statement III is false: pyridine (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 5) is far too weak to deprotonate ethanol (pKa ≈ 16), and none is needed because acid chlorides react with neutral alcohols. Answer: I and II only.
x: Statement II is also correct: pyridine is a good nucleophile toward acid chlorides, and the acylpyridinium ion it forms is even more reactive.
Statement III is false: an acid chloride is reactive enough to acylate neutral ethanol, and pyridine is too weak a base to make ethoxide.
Statement III is false, so all three cannot be right.

q: Aniline reacts with acetic anhydride. Besides acetic acid, what organic product forms?
h: An anhydride transfers one acyl group; the other half leaves as a carboxylate (then acid).
w: Aniline's nitrogen attacks one carbonyl; the tetrahedral intermediate expels acetate, and proton transfer gives A: acetanilide (N-phenylacetamide) plus acetic acid.
x: Only one acyl group is transferred to nitrogen; the second acetyl leaves as acetate, so a diacetylated amine is not the product (and no water is formed).
Anhydrides acylate the nitrogen; they do not do Friedel–Crafts acylation of the ring without a Lewis acid, and the NH<sub>2</sub> group would react first anyway.
Aniline is not converted to phenol, and acetamide is not formed; the amine nitrogen becomes the amide nitrogen.

q: Succinic anhydride is warmed in methanol (no catalyst). What is the main product?
h: A cyclic anhydride opens after one acyl substitution. Where does the leaving group end up?
w: Methanol attacks one carbonyl of the cyclic anhydride. When the tetrahedral intermediate collapses, the leaving carboxylate is still tethered to the molecule, so the ring opens and one end becomes a methyl ester while the other becomes a carboxylic acid: A, 4-methoxy-4-oxobutanoic acid (monomethyl succinate).
x: The second CO<sub>2</sub>H would need Fischer esterification (acid catalyst, heat) to become an ester; a carboxylic acid is much less reactive than the anhydride.
Ring opening with water would give succinic acid; here methanol is the nucleophile, so one end becomes CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
γ-Butyrolactone would require reduction of one carbonyl; no reducing agent is present.

q: Benzoic acid and methylamine are mixed in ether at room temperature. What forms?
h: Before any acyl substitution can happen, what does an amine do with a carboxylic acid?
w: The fastest reaction between a carboxylic acid (pKa 4.2) and an amine (conjugate acid pKa ≈ 10.6) is proton transfer, giving methylammonium benzoate. The carboxylate is too unreactive to be attacked, so making the amide needs strong heating to drive off water, or better, conversion to an acid chloride (SOCl2) or activation with DCC first.
x: Direct amide formation from the acid and amine requires prolonged heating above ~150 °C (or a coupling agent); at room temperature only the salt forms.
No ester can form without an alcohol, and the amine nitrogen does not give up its methyl group.
There is no chlorine source; acid chlorides are made with SOCl<sub>2</sub>, (COCl)<sub>2</sub> or PCl<sub>5</sub>.

q: Which sequence converts butanoic acid into hexan-3-one, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
h: Count carbons: the acid supplies four, including the future C=O. What must be added, and which organometallic stops at the ketone?
w: Hexan-3-one = butanoyl (4 C, with the C=O) + ethyl (2 C). Convert the acid to butanoyl chloride with SOCl2, then add one ethyl with the Gilman reagent, which does not add again to the ketone: 1. SOCl2 2. (CH3CH2)2CuLi.
x: Excess Grignard adds twice to an acid chloride, giving the 3° alcohol 3-ethylhexan-3-ol, not the ketone.
A Grignard reagent simply deprotonates the carboxylic acid (giving ethane and a carboxylate salt); no C–C bond forms.
Dimethylcuprate adds a methyl, not an ethyl, giving pentan-2-one (five carbons), one carbon short.

q: 4-Aminophenol is treated with one equivalent of acetic anhydride. What is the major product?
h: Which is the stronger nucleophile, an aryl NH<sub>2</sub> or a phenol OH? With only one equivalent, which reacts?
w: Both groups can be acylated, but nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so its lone pair is more available: the amine is far more nucleophilic than the neutral phenol. With one equivalent of anhydride, N-acetylation wins, giving A, N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide (acetaminophen). The amide product is also more stable than an aryl ester.
x: O-Acetylation of the phenol is slower because a neutral OH is a weaker nucleophile than NH<sub>2</sub>; this ester is not the major product.
Diacetylation needs at least two equivalents of anhydride; with one equivalent the more nucleophilic N reacts selectively.
Ring acylation (Friedel–Crafts) needs a Lewis acid such as AlCl<sub>3</sub>; an anhydride alone acylates N or O, not the ring carbon.
